arabian-1: Opening-only observation: a prosperous ruler dies leaving two closely bonded sons. Their succession establishes the dynastic frame for the linked collection, rather than an independently extracted complete tale.
arabian-2: Opening-only observation: a wealthy merchant crosses a foodless desert on business, carrying modest provisions. His return journey supplies the setting for the coming encounter.
arabian-3: Opening-only observation: a traveller identifies a hind as his transformed wife and introduces an adopted heir. The household's concealed hostility creates a caregiving conflict before his departure.
arabian-4: Opening-only observation: three brothers inherit equal sums and become merchants. One converts his assets into goods for foreign travel, establishing contrasting choices about a shared opportunity.
arabian-5: Opening-only observation: an ageing fisherman struggles to support his household and limits himself to four daily net casts. An unexpectedly heavy first catch raises hope before its identity is revealed.
arabian-6: Opening-only observation: a ruler's illness has resisted treatment. A newly arrived physician offers a different method; this is historical fantasy, not evidence-based medical guidance.
arabian-7: Opening-only observation: a departing husband purchases a reporting parrot to monitor his wife. The setup involves surveillance and mistrust, not an approved model of a supportive relationship.
arabian-8: Opening-only observation: a prince hunts under a minister's supervision but pursues a deer alone. Losing both the quarry and his escort turns excitement into disorientation.
arabian-9: Opening-only observation: a young ruler describes inheriting an island kingdom and marrying his cousin. A conversation overheard while resting introduces uncertainty about the relationship.
arabian-10: Opening-only observation: a Baghdad porter waits for work with his basket. A veiled customer hires him to follow her, beginning the encounter that frames several visitors' stories.
arabian-11: Opening-only observation: a royal narrator promises to explain his lost eye and changed clothing. Repeated visits to a neighbouring uncle's court establish a close cousin relationship before the incident.
arabian-12: Opening-only observation: a royal narrator explains his unusual education before recounting the loss of an eye. The historical religious curriculum is descriptive source context, not certified instruction.
arabian-13: Opening-only observation: a man's neighbour develops persistent envy and hostility. The target sells his home and moves away, hoping distance will dissolve the conflict.
arabian-14: Opening-only observation: a new ruler attributes his lost eye to his own actions. He first describes inspecting mainland provinces and neighbouring islands after succession.
arabian-15: Opening-only observation: a poor porter rests outside a comfortable house after carrying a heavy load in the heat. The contrast in circumstances introduces the frame for seven voyage narratives.
arabian-16: Opening-only observation: a young heir wastes much of his fortune, then sells household goods and joins traders. The first voyage begins as a practical response to dwindling resources.
arabian-17: Opening-only observation: a returned traveller grows restless despite his plan to remain at home. He prepares trade goods and sails again with known merchants.
arabian-18: Opening-only observation: successful voyages no longer deter a merchant from sailing. Another profitable expedition encounters a dangerous wind, changing the journey's prospects.
arabian-19: Opening-only observation: curiosity and trade draw a wealthy merchant out again. After arranging goods across several destinations, he embarks from a distant port and meets a hurricane.
arabian-20: Opening-only observation: a traveller chooses a ship of his own to control its itinerary. He invites other merchants to share the voyage while seeking new experiences.
arabian-21: Opening-only observation: after a year's rest, a traveller ignores loved ones' attempts to keep him home. An overland approach to a new departure port begins his sixth voyage.
arabian-22: Opening-only observation: a veteran traveller resolves to retire peacefully, but a ruler's officer summons him. Public duty interrupts his chosen quiet life.
arabian-23: Opening-only observation: a tailor enjoys a visitor's music and invites him home to entertain his wife. The historical portrayal of disability requires review, not repetition of the edition's demeaning framing.
arabian-24: Opening-only observation: an idle son receives a share of a small inheritance and must decide how to use unfamiliar capital. His uncertainty begins the narrated brother's story.
arabian-25: Opening-only observation: a man loses his inherited money and survives by seeking help. Social skill and relationships with household servants provide access to wealthier patrons.
arabian-26: Opening-only observation: a prosperous island ruler considers himself fortunate but lacks an heir. The royal household's unmet succession wish introduces a long romance narrative, not a preschool concept.
arabian-27: Opening-only observation: a ruler appoints two ministers to administer his kingdom. One is described as generous and helpful, establishing a contrast in official conduct.
arabian-28: Opening-only observation: an unemployed youth continues playing after his father's death. A stranger asks about his identity and deceased parent, introducing a potentially exploitative approach.
arabian-29: Opening-only observation: a bored ruler waits in his palace while an experienced minister arrives with important business. Their encounter frames a search for diversion.
arabian-30: Opening-only observation: an orphan builds a modest inheritance into a profitable camel-hiring business. Frequent journeys and increasing assets establish the narrator's circumstances before his crisis.
arabian-31: Opening-only observation: a ruler challenges a young man about cruel treatment of his horse. The demand for an explanation frames the account without excusing animal harm.
arabian-32: Opening-only observation: a contented merchant repeatedly dreams of a reproach about delayed pilgrimage. He becomes troubled by the recurring message; religious obligations require qualified review.
arabian-33: Opening-only observation: during a royal New Year celebration, a visitor presents an apparently lifelike horse. The interruption creates curiosity about an unfamiliar invention.
arabian-34: Opening-only observation: a newly crowned ruler disguises himself to seek city adventures, accompanied by his minister. Their departure establishes a hidden-identity frame before the sisters' story.
egypt-modern-1: Opening-only observation: a childless ruler accepts a visitor's promise of a son in return for surrendering that first child. The bargain establishes an obligation, not a verified medical or religious claim.
egypt-modern-2: Opening-only observation: a ruler steals a flying maiden's feather garment and agrees to harm his existing wives to secure her presence. This coercive setup is historical source material, not a child-safe model.
egypt-modern-3: Opening-only observation: a ruler demands that his minister find a mood-regulating seal within three days. Local craftsmen cannot supply it, so the minister seeks advice elsewhere.
egypt-modern-4: Opening-only observation: a fisherman becomes ill and his wife helps with fishing near the palace. A ruler's desire for her introduces a threat against the husband.
egypt-modern-5: Opening-only observation: a princess raises an unusually large louse in an oil vessel. Its extraordinary size becomes part of a royal marriage challenge; the full causal resolution remains unextracted.
egypt-modern-6: Opening-only observation: travelling merchant parents leave their daughter in a judge's care. This establishes a vulnerable caregiving arrangement; the source needs safeguarding review rather than assumptions of benevolent authority.
egypt-modern-7: Opening-only observation: a prince rejects a marriage arranged solely by his father and travels in disguise. An encounter with a farming family begins his search for a partner.
egypt-modern-8: Opening-only observation: a woman's wish for a daughter includes a dangerous condition associated with flax. A prince's attraction to the young girl leads to an intermediary's intervention; no child-romance adaptation is approved.
egypt-modern-9: Opening-only observation: a poor musician needs money after his child's birth. Finding an egg prompts a trading plan and an encounter with a purchaser; historical identity portrayals require separate review.
egypt-modern-10: Opening-only observation: brothers build a palace for their sister, who seeks advice about her restrictions. An old woman's suggestion introduces a quest for a singing bird.
egypt-modern-11: Opening-only observation: a ruler and minister overhear three women describe remarkable gifts they could provide through marriage. Their claims establish a fantastical royal-choice premise, not factual human abilities.
egypt-modern-12: Opening-only observation: a prince grows up alongside a horse born at the same time. After his mother's death and his father's remarriage, the horse warns him of a poisoning threat.
egypt1-1: Opening-only observation: a king asks his sons for accounts of magicians. Their embedded stories introduce wondrous performances and royal succession; each episode requires separate extraction and faith-sensitive adaptation.
egypt1-2: Opening-only observation: a travelling peasant's laden animals encounter a landholder's obstructive arrangement. A dispute over damage and property develops into an appeal to authority.
egypt1-3: A shipwreck survivor meets a supernatural island host who foretells rescue and supplies gifts. The sailor returns toward home, using the remembered encounter to encourage another traveller facing authority.
egypt1-4: Opening-only observation: a court follower hears urgent news after a ruler's death and flees. His departure begins a long displacement narrative whose eventual return is recorded in this historical translation.
egypt2-1: A commander conceals soldiers inside loads presented as tribute. Once admitted through the city gates, they emerge and capture its inhabitants. The strategy belongs to a violent military tale, not endorsed child behaviour.
egypt2-2: A prince is warned of three possible fatal threats and later survives a serpent through his wife's intervention. The surviving papyrus stops during a crocodile encounter, so no final escape or death is supplied.
egypt2-3: Opening-only observation: two brothers share farm work and a household, with the younger undertaking much of the labour. Their relationship sets up a complex betrayal-and-transformation story, not a simple sibling cooperation template.
egypt2-4: Opening-only observation: a learned prince searches a tomb for a powerful book. Its custodians warn him against taking it, establishing a conflict between desired knowledge and responsibility toward its owners.
kalila-1: Opening-only observation: rulers and a philosopher frame the commissioning and transmission of a book of counsel. The chapter grounds a knowledge-seeking frame, not an invented animal fable.
kalila-2: Opening-only observation: a court seeks a valuable book through a learned envoy's journey to India. The chapter links knowledge acquisition with service and gratitude; its religious introduction remains a review flag.
westafrica-1: Anansi wants ownership of the tales and accepts three capture tasks. He exploits each animal's curiosity or pride to complete them, winning the naming privilege through deceptive ingenuity.
westafrica-2: Anansi tries to hide all wisdom in a pot but cannot climb with it hanging in front. His son's practical suggestion disproves his monopoly; the broken pot releases wisdom to everyone.
westafrica-3: Anansi borrows a wealthy neighbour's clothes to impress prospective wives. When the deception unravels, jealousy leads to a fatal trap and a bereaved wife's appeal for shared mourning.
westafrica-4: Anansi hides a food-producing gift from his hungry family. After they discover and exhaust it, he seeks another gift but receives a punishing stick, turning selfish repetition into painful consequence.
westafrica-5: Anansi obtains secret royal names, but his herald receives the promised reward. He retaliates by planting evidence and disabling the herald's speech, producing an unjust judgement rather than an acceptable lesson.
westafrica-8: Anansi uses a newly built road as false proof that another creature's farm is his. A crow later applies equally dubious ownership reasoning to the stolen harvest, reversing his gain.
westafrica-9: A son receives rain through a gentle request, while Anansi's forceful imitation kills the helper. He shifts a lasting burden onto a trusting ant; the source's violence and deception require redesign.
westafrica-10: Anansi secretly consumes a harvest earned by his whole household. The family builds a sticky decoy to catch the thief, and repeated blows trap him until his identity is exposed.
nasreddin-1: A speaker repeatedly asks whether listeners know his message. Each response gives him a reason not to preach, ending with a proposal that knowledgeable listeners teach the others.
nasreddin-2: A speaker imagines the damage that winged camels could cause by landing on rooftops. His comic gratitude depends on an impossible animal feature, not a scientific or theological explanation.
nasreddin-3: A traveller claims two cities have identical air because the stars look equally numerous. The joke rests on an unsupported inference from one observation to a different property.
nasreddin-4: A dreamer negotiates for more imaginary money and wakes with nothing. He closes his eyes again, hoping that accepting the earlier offer might recover a vanished bargain.
nasreddin-5: A frightened traveller hides in a tomb when horsemen approach. When they ask why he is there, he invents an explanation about being a buried person taking a walk.
nasreddin-6: Caught taking vegetables, a visitor blames the wind for his presence and the uprooted crops. A question about his filled sack exposes the limits of the improvised excuse.
nasreddin-7: A visitor takes a pastry without paying and is struck by its maker. He reframes the blows as part of local dining custom; theft and punishment are not endorsed adaptation goals.
nasreddin-8: A man counts fasting days by putting stones in a pot. Extra stones added by his daughter corrupt the count, and his attempted compromise still produces an impossible calendar date.
nasreddin-9: Asked what happens to the old moon, a speaker invents that it becomes stars. The short answer is comic fabrication, not astronomy or religious instruction.
nasreddin-10: A traveller mounts a caravan camel for comfort, is thrown, and is rescued by companions. He responds with a violent demand against the animal rather than understanding the danger.
nasreddin-11: A trader buys nine eggs for a coin and sells ten for the same price. Challenged about the loss, he claims the disadvantage is deliberately displayed to his friends.
nasreddin-12: A man steals and kills a neighbour's animal, then jokes about the owner's distress. This historical anecdote offers no reparative ending and is not default child-family material.
nasreddin-13: Asked about the moon's current phase, a passer-by declines because he neither buys nor sells it. He substitutes commercial relevance for the astronomical question.
nasreddin-14: A man climbs into a garden with a ladder and claims to be selling it when challenged. His excuse shifts the issue from unauthorized entry to where goods can be sold.
nasreddin-15: A man dresses living birds in tokens of mourning and explains that their mothers were slaughtered. The joke personifies grief around killing rather than providing a gentle bedtime situation.
